messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Phommasack is a 26-year-old Lao-American man who works as a bank teller at a mid-sized branch in a suburban strip mall. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief conversation with his primary care physician, who noted that Kiet had lost considerable weight and described sleeping "maybe two or three hours a night." Kiet is recently divorced and lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment. He presented to the intake session with a flat affect and a habit of positioning his chair so that his back faced the wall — something he did without apparent awareness until it was gently noted.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Kiet was working his regular shift when two armed men entered the bank and initiated a robbery that escalated into a prolonged hostage situation. During the ordeal, which lasted nearly four hours, Kiet was ordered at gunpoint to open his drawer and assist in moving customers to the back of the branch. At one point, one of the perpetrators struck a colleague across the face when she moved too slowly. Kiet was standing close enough to hear the impact. What stayed with him — what still replays with a quality he describes as "happening right now, not like a memory" — was the moment he complied with the gunman's instructions to push a frightened elderly customer toward the back, physically steering her by the shoulders while she wept. He did what he was told. He has not forgiven himself for it.

In the weeks following the incident, Kiet began to notice that the ordinary geography of his job had become saturated with threat. The sound of the branch door opening, the sight of someone in a hood or with their hands in their pockets, the particular angle of light through the front windows in the late afternoon — each of these had become a signal. He began checking behind him constantly while walking from the parking lot to the entrance, certain that the sensation of being watched was not paranoia but information. He woke most nights between two and four in the morning and moved through his apartment checking the locks, the windows, the closet. He was irritable in ways that frightened him — snapping at customers over minor delays, raising his voice once at a colleague in a manner that left them both shaken.

What made this worse, in a way that felt almost circular, was what Kiet had come to believe about himself. He was certain he was no longer the person he had been before the robbery — someone who had prided himself on steadiness, on being the calm one in a crisis. He had acted in a way that violated something central to his sense of himself, and that conviction sat in him like a stone. He could not rely on his own judgment or his own instincts anymore. And it was precisely this belief — that he was compromised, untrustworthy, diminished — that kept his nervous system in a state of permanent vigilance, as though his body had concluded that if he couldn't trust himself to act well under pressure, he had better watch everything else twice as carefully. The hypervigilance, in turn, confirmed his worst appraisals: every night check, every flinch at the door, every moment of irrational anger at the teller window felt like further evidence that he was broken.

Kiet responded to this by working longer hours. He volunteered for extra shifts, stayed late reconciling accounts, and filled his evenings with tasks that kept his hands and eyes occupied. At first this seemed to help, but over months it deepened his isolation and quietly reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of a normal life — that he needed to be constantly busy simply to function, that stillness was something he had lost the right to. His marriage, already strained in the aftermath of the attack, ended when his wife told him she could no longer reach him. He had made himself unreachable; he had understood this even as he did it.

Kiet came to seek help after a customer at the bank — a young man in a dark jacket who reached suddenly into his bag — caused Kiet to step backward and knock over a display stand. His manager spoke to him privately afterward. What Kiet told the intake clinician he was most afraid of was that there was nothing left to recover — that the person who had walked into that bank fourteen months ago had simply not walked back out.
